o: Rearrange nums so absolute values are non-decreasing; any valid arrangement is accepted. Example: [3,-1,-4,1,5] → [-1,1,3,-4,5]. With n ≤ 100 almost anything works; the interesting part is doing it without extra space.
k: Any stable or unstable ordering by |value| is accepted — ties may appear in any order.
Two natural solutions: a comparator sort, or a counting/bucket pass exploiting the tiny value range (-100..100).

a.i: Sort with key = absolute value. Simplest correct solution.
a.sp: O(1)–O(n) depending on language sort internals.

a.i: Values lie in [-100, 100], so count occurrences of each absolute value 0..100 and rebuild the array, emitting negatives before positives (or any order) per bucket.
s: Tally cnt[a] = number of elements with |value| = a.
For a from 0 to 100, append -a cnt[a] times (if a > 0) then a cnt[a] times.
a.t: O(n + R) where R = 101 is the value range — linear counting sort.

w: Trivial warm-up; mention the counting-sort variant to show range awareness. Pitfall: in Java you cannot sort a primitive int[] with a comparator directly — box it or write counting sort. Follow-up: sort by absolute value stably, or handle a much wider value range (then comparator sort wins).
